notes.read: A gray tabby curled asleep on a yellow knitted blanket on a sunny windowsill. What matters is the cat's round sleeping shape and its stripes; what's hard is the knit, which has to be one repeated stitch mark. The background is a few flat areas, so the time goes on the blanket and the cat.

stages.name: Blend the pale sky in the window
steps: Start at the top left corner of the canvas with Pale sky blue, the sky through the window.
Stroke side to side across the corner. Without rinsing, pick up Warm white and paint lower down, then stroke back up over the join a few times while both are wet.
Keep the blue strongest along the top edge and let it fade to nearly white lower down. The patch's middle is about 1 1/4 in from the left edge and 1 1/4 in from the top edge.
The rest of the canvas stays bare until step 4.
Stop when the sky is a soft blue-to-white patch in the corner, its lower edge loose and uneven, not a ruled line.

stages.name: Dab the green leaves outside
steps: Let the sky dry first, or the green will smear into it.
Start in the lower part of the pale sky, near the left edge of the canvas, about 2 in from the top edge.
Wipe most of the paint off the brush, then tap with its tip. Tap the middle of the clump more times so it gets solid, and fewer taps at its rim.
Keep it to one small, ragged clump about 1 1/4 in wide. These are far leaves outside, so no single leaves, just dappled green.
Leave pale sky showing around the clump and in a few small gaps between the dabs.
Stop at one soft green clump, solid in the middle and broken at the edges. Blobs mean the brush is too wet.

stages.name: Tap the sunny leaves
steps: Let the dark green dabs from step 2 dry first.
Start on the top of the green clump, the side toward the light.
The same tapping as the dark leaves, now with a lighter green and only where the sun hits the clump.
With a nearly dry brush, tap lightly with the tip, a few taps in each spot so the dots stay broken.
Put most of the taps on the upper part of the clump where the sun hits, and a couple of small taps lower down in the sky.
Leave the darker green showing under and between the light taps, and the pale sky around them.
Stop after a few small yellow-green patches. The clump should read as sunny on top and shaded below, not as one flat green.

stages.name: Criss-cross the blue wall
steps: Let the sky and the leaves dry first.
Use short criss-cross strokes, like overlapping Xs, with Wall blue and some Light wall blue on the brush together, varying how much of each.
Cover the wall down to a slanted line where the sill will start. Lay a narrow band of Wall blue alone at the inner corner, and run blue down beside and under the sky.
Leave the pale sky and leaves showing. The bottom of the canvas stays bare until step 7.
Stop when the wall is a loose, textured blue with lighter patches, criss-cross marks showing, and a darker upright strip at the inner corner.

stages.name: Block in the white frame
steps: Let the blue wall dry first, so the white stays clean.
Start with the tall post, a long rectangle from the top edge down, its middle about 1 3/4 in from the left edge.
Paint each piece as a rectangle with straight pulls along its length: the post, then a crossbar across the window, then the ledge under it.
The crossbar cuts the window view in two, and the ledge slants down toward the wall's corner. Keep the frame's pieces straight and fairly narrow.
Leave the sky and leaves showing in the two window openings, and the dark blue strip at the inner corner.
Stop when the frame is flat creamy white with fairly straight edges and no shading.

stages.name: Shade the frame lavender
steps: Let the white frame dry first.
Start on the face of the post that turns toward the blue wall, from the top edge down.
You build from pieces again, but this time as narrow strips with a smaller brush, only on the frame's shaded faces.
Lay each shadow as a narrow strip with straight pulls along the piece: down the post's side, along the underside of the crossbar, and along the lower edge of the ledge.
Shade the faces turned away from the window light. The widest shadow runs down the post's side, where it turns toward the blue wall.
Leave the fronts of the post, the crossbar and the ledge creamy white, where the light from the window hits them.
Stop when the frame has soft lavender strips on its shadow faces, so it looks deep rather than flat.

stages.name: Block in the wooden sill
steps: Let the wall and the frame dry first.
Start along the slanted line where the blue wall stops, and work down.
Built from rectangles like the frame, but with the big brush and just two broad pieces: the flat shelf and its front edge.
Lay the sill as two big pieces: a wide band for its top, then a strip along the bottom edge for its front, pulling the brush side to side across the canvas.
Cover the whole bottom of the canvas from the left edge to the right edge and down to the bottom edge, in one even rust brown.
Leave the wall, the frame and its ledge untouched, with a clean slanted join where the sill meets them.
Stop when the bottom of the canvas is a flat rust-brown sill with no shading or sun patches.

stages.name: Press in the dark stitches
steps: Let the flat yellow roll from step 10 dry first.
Start at the rounded left end of the roll, on its top row.
Touch the tip down, press, then pull and lift so each stitch is a small teardrop. Set them in pairs leaning toward each other, like Vs, in rows along the length of the roll.
Fill the whole roll with rows, following its curve around the left end. Crowd them darker along the fold low on the roll and along its bottom, where the light doesn't reach.
Leave the flat yellow from step 10 showing between all the stitches.
Stop when the whole roll is covered in rows of dark V stitches, with a clear darker fold line running along its lower part.

steps: Let the white patches dry first.
Start at the top of the back, near the upright ear, with the first body stripe.
Press the full brush down at the spine, then pull down around the curve of the body, turning onto the edge so each stripe tapers toward the belly. On the tail, pull short bars across it.

Leave gray between the stripes, and keep the white muzzle, paws and chest patch clean.
Stop when dark tabby stripes wrap the body, tail and head, thick at the top and thin at the ends.

Start with the closed eye low on the face, the eye nearest the window.

opening.welcome: You are about to paint a gray tabby cat fast asleep, curled on a chunky yellow blanket on a sunny windowsill. The heart of it is the sleeping face: the closed eyes, the pink nose and the white muzzle by the paws. Keep it warm and soft, and let the cat feel cozy.
opening.light: Daylight comes in through the window. It brightens the cat's face and the near end of the blanket, throws peach sun patches across the sill, and leaves the cat's far end and back in shadow.

skills.how: You build a shape from simple pieces: one rectangle or oval first, then curved or straight pieces added on. It makes the frame, the sill, the blanket roll and the whole cat. Leave the pieces showing unless the shape needs to look smooth.

Touch the tip down, press so the brush spreads, then pull and lift so the mark ends in a point. It makes every knit stitch on the blanket, the pink in the ears and the tiny nose. Too much paint or a slow lift gives a blob instead of a teardrop.
Only the tip goes in the paint, with no water, and you skim the canvas lightly. It gives the sill its broken shadows and its glowing sun patch. If it goes on solid, the brush was too loaded.

opening.road: We paint from the back of the scene to the front. First comes the view through the window and the blue wall, then the white frame and the wooden sill, so the room is finished before anything sits in it. Next the blanket goes on as a flat roll, and its knit stitches are pressed in dark, then light. The cat goes on last, over everything: a flat gray shape, its shading and white patches, then its stripes, ears and fur. The lesson ends on the sleeping face, with the eyes, the nose and the whiskers. Early layers leave bare canvas where later stages will cover it, so don't worry about the white you see.

the-window-view.for: A soft pale sky and a clump of far leaves, seen through the window.
the-window-view.end: A small blue sky patch with a soft green clump of leaves sits in the corner, and the rest of the canvas is still bare.

the-wall.for: A loose, textured blue wall that fills the room behind the cat.
the-wall.end: The criss-crossed blue wall now wraps the window view, with a darker strip at the inner corner, and the rest of the canvas is still bare.

the-window-frame.for: A white window frame that looks deep, with lavender shadows on its shaded faces.
the-window-frame.end: A creamy white frame with lavender shadows stands between the window view and the blue wall, and the rest of the canvas is still bare.

the-sill.for: A wooden sill that the cat's blanket rests on, with shadow and a patch of sunlight.
the-sill.end: The room is finished: a rust-brown sill with darker streaks and a glowing peach sun patch meets the wall and the window.

the-blanket.for: A chunky knitted blanket roll, stitched dark and then light.
the-blanket.end: A golden knitted roll lies across the sill, its stitches darker in the fold and lighter where the window light hits.

the-cat-shape.for: The cat's whole shape, its rounded shading and its white patches.
the-cat-shape.end: A rounded gray cat lies curled on the blanket, with a white muzzle, white paws and a white chest patch.

the-markings.for: The tabby stripes, the pink ears and soft fur that make the cat read as a tabby.
the-markings.end: The cat has dark tabby stripes, pink ears and soft fur on its head, but its face is still blank.

the-face.for: The sleeping face: closed eyes, a pink nose and white whiskers.
the-face.end: The painting is finished: a tabby cat fast asleep on its yellow blanket in the window light.

technique_picks.technique_why: A cozy indoor scene of big simple shapes (a window, a wall, a sill, a blanket and one curled cat) suits painting back to front, with the cat built from an oval and finished in passes.
